CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 32




              BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA


          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION                     )
          OF OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC                         )
          COMPANY FOR AN ORDER OF THE                          )
          COMMISSION APPROVING NEW EXTRA                       )
          LARGE LOAD TARIFF AND TERMS AND                      )       CASE NO. PUD 2026-000046
          CONDITIONS OF SERVICE FOR EXTRA                      )
          LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS AND A                           )
          REGULATORY ASSET TO RECOVER                          )
          COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH PORTFOLIO                      )
          OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE


                             BRIEF IN CHIEF OF GOOGLE REGARDING
                          ALTERNATIVE ELECTRIC SERVICE FRAMEWORKS

                Google LLC (“Google”), respectfully submit this Joint Brief in Chief pursuant to Order

         No. 761449, issued October 21, 2026, by the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (“Commission”)

         in the above-captioned proceeding concerning Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company's (“OG&E”)

         proposed Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) Tariff. The Commission established

         supplemental briefing to address substantial legal and jurisdictional issues concerning alternative

         electric service frameworks raised in this proceeding. The Commission should recognize its

         authority to consider BYONG or self-supply arrangements under Oklahoma's existing regulatory

         framework, while reserving determination of the merits of any particular proposal for

         consideration of the evidentiary record and should reject OG&E's contrary legal arguments.

                                     I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

                The issue presented is whether the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (“Commission”)

         has legal authority to consider and approve retail electric service arrangements accommodating

         self-supply, or Bring Your Own New Generation (“BYONG”), including arrangements in which




                                                         1
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 32




         a retail customer procures generation through transactions in federally regulated wholesale markets

         while continuing to receive retail service from its incumbent certificated utility. It does.

                 Article IX, Section 18 of the Oklahoma Constitution vests the Commission with broad

         authority to supervise, regulate, and control public utilities, including the authority to prescribe

         rates, charges, and rules of service.1 That authority includes establishing rate schedules,

         classifications, and terms of service that reflect customers’ particular characteristics and the costs

         of serving them. A tariff does not become unlawful merely because it distinguishes between

         generation furnished by the incumbent and generation a customer procures through a lawful

         wholesale arrangement.

                 Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E”) advances a contrary theory in this

         proceeding. In its rebuttal testimony, OG&E characterizes proposals permitting large load

         customers to obtain generation outside its bundled service framework as “Delivery Only

         Deregulated Generation Election,” proposals and asserts that they are legally infirm and threaten

         Oklahoma’s integrated regulatory framework.2 Three points answer that contention.

                 First, the Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act (“RESCTA”) regulates the

         furnishing of retail electric service within certificated territories.3 Its operative concern is the

         identity of the entity furnishing retail electric service to the consuming facility. A separate

         wholesale generation arrangement does not establish that a competing retail supplier has entered

         the incumbent's territory where the incumbent certificated utility retains the retail relationship,

         administers the applicable Commission-approved tariff, provides delivery service, meters and bills

         the customer's load, and remains responsible for the retail services it undertakes to provide.



         1
           Okla. Const. art. IX, § 18; 17 O.S. §§ 152-153.
         2
           Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop, Entry No. 64, pp. 2-3.
         3
           17 O.S. §§ 158.21-158.32.


                                                                2
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 32




                 Second, the Federal Power Act places wholesale sales of electric energy in interstate

         commerce within the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”), while

         preserving state jurisdiction over retail electric service and other matters reserved to the states.

         Transactions conducted through the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) Integrated Marketplace must

         therefore be analyzed according to their actual legal and operational characteristics, rather than

         simply characterized as retail transactions because the energy ultimately supports an end-use

         customer's load.

                 Third, House Bill 2992 (17 O.S. §§ 901-905) requires cost-causation-based tariffs for

         qualifying large load customers and neither prohibits customer self-supply nor displaces the

         Commission's constitutional and statutory ratemaking authority, while the Commission's threshold

         legal authority to approve a self-supply framework remains distinct from its evidentiary evaluation

         of specific tariff terms.

                 Oklahoma law does not categorically prohibit the Commission from approving

         appropriately structured retail electric service arrangements accommodating customer self-supply

         while preserving the incumbent’s certificated retail service relationship.

                 In Order No. 761449, the Commission established a supplemental briefing schedule to

         address substantial legal and jurisdictional issues raised in this proceeding. The Order identified a

         set of legal questions, designated items (a) through (n), that may assist the Commission in resolving

         the issues presented.4 Google submits this Brief in Chief as proponents of alternative electric

         service frameworks under the amended schedule and address each of those items: item (a) in Parts

         III and IV; item (b) in Part V; item (e) in Part VI; items (g) and (h) in Part VII; items (c) and (d)

         in Part VIII; items (f) and (i) in Part IX; items (j) through (m) in Part X; and item (n) in Part XI


         4
          Order Granting Motion to Amend the Procedural Schedule in Order No. 758969 to Include a Briefing Schedule,
         Order No. 761449 (Okla. Corp. Comm’n Oct. 21, 2026) (“Order No. 761449”), at 2–3.


                                                               3
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 32




         and Part VII.D. Part II first explains what customer self-supply is, how it operates within SPP, and

         what it is not.

                     II. WHAT CUSTOMER SELF-SUPPLY IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT

                 A. The structure of a self-supply or BYONG arrangement.

                 A self-supply or BYONG option permits a large load customer to procure some or all of

         the generation capacity and energy necessary to serve its load from resources other than the

         incumbent utility’s generation fleet, while continuing to take retail electric service from the

         incumbent. The customer’s procurement is accomplished through bilateral wholesale power

         purchase agreements or customer-owned or third-party generation resources interconnected to the

         SPP transmission system that deliver SPP-accredited capacity (including the required SPP

         Planning Reserve Margin) and wholesale energy into the SPP Integrated Marketplace.

                 Whatever the form, three features of the arrangement are constant. First, the customer is

         still served exclusively by the incumbent’s facilities, through the incumbent’s meter, under the

         incumbent’s tariff. Second, the generator delivers into the SPP Integrated Marketplace rather than

         directly to the customer’s premises. Third, the incumbent remains the load-responsible entity for

         the customer’s entire load in SPP, and the customer’s supply is registered, accredited, and settled

         through that relationship.

                 B. What remains with the incumbent.

                 Every attribute that defines retail electric service remains with the incumbent. The

         incumbent holds the certificate for the territory in which the customer’s facility is located. It serves

         the customer under a Commission-approved retail tariff, pursuant to a written service agreement,

         at a defined delivery point and voltage. It constructs, owns, and operates the delivery facilities,

         even where the customer funds them through a contribution in aid of construction. It meters the




                                                            4
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 32




         customer’s total load and renders the bill. It administers every commercial term of the retail

         relationship: contract term, billing demand, minimum bill, collateral, and exit provisions (if

         applicable). No third party holds a certificate, owns or operates facilities delivering energy to the

         premises, meters the load, renders a bill, administers a tariff, or has any retail service relationship

         with the customer.

                    C. What self-supply is not.

                    A self-supply or BYONG option does not certify a new retail supplier, open any customer

         class to competitive retail supply, remove any customer from Commission-approved tariff service,

         or require the incumbent to transmit power on behalf of a third party to a retail customer. It does

         not deregulate generation; the incumbent’s generation fleet remains rate-regulated and continues

         to serve every customer that takes utility generation service. It does not alter SPP resource

         adequacy obligations; it allocates the cost of meeting them. And it does not depend on any FERC

         action, waiver, or authorization.

                       III. PROCEDURAL POSTURE AND BURDEN OF PROOF (ITEM (a))

                    The Commission has emphasized that the burden of proof lies with the Applicant.5 OG&E

         bears the burden of demonstrating that the rates, terms, and conditions it proposes for large load

         customers are just, reasonable, and in the public interest. It does not discharge that burden by

         attacking the alternatives advanced by other parties, and it holds no veto over the outcome of its

         own application. In fixing just and reasonable rates, the Commission is not confined to choosing

         between the applicant’s proposal and denial; it exercises independent judgment on the whole

         record and may adopt, modify, or reject any proposal, or prescribe rates and terms of its own.6




         5
             Order No. 761449 at 2.
         6
             Okla. Const. art. IX, § 18; 17 O.S. §§ 151–152; OAC 165:5-13.


                                                                  5
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 32




                 The Commission has also noted that this preliminary legal briefing is specific to the

         circumstances of this proceeding and not precedent for future cases, and that the enumerated topics

         do not limit the issues or the positions parties may present.7 Google addresses each enumerated

         item below, and address additional issues under item (n) in Part XI.

             IV. THE COMMISSION POSSESSES BROAD CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY
              AUTHORITY TO APPROVE RETAIL ELECTRIC SERVICE FRAMEWORKS THAT
                   ACCOMMODATE CUSTOMER SELF-SUPPLY OR BYONG (ITEM (a))

                 A. The Commission's authority to approve retail tariffs encompasses alternative
                 service arrangements, including self-supply and BYONG.

                 Article IX, Section 18 of the Oklahoma Constitution vests the Commission with general

         authority to supervise, regulate, and control public utilities, including the authority to prescribe

         rates, charges, and rules of service.8

                 The Legislature has implemented that grant by vesting the Commission with general power

         to supervise and regulate every public utility and to fix and enforce just and reasonable rates.9 The

         Commission’s authority to design rates and to establish classes of service is well settled; the

         limitation recognized by the Oklahoma Supreme Court is that the Commission must act within its

         constitutional and statutory bounds.10

                 The Commission exercises that authority whenever it determines the rates and conditions

         under which an electric utility furnishes service to its customers. Such authority necessarily

         includes the ability to recognize differences among customer classes, establish appropriate billing

         determinants, assign costs according to the services rendered, and approve tariff provisions

         reflecting the particular needs and characteristics of the customers being served.



         7
           Order No. 761449 at 2–3.
         8
           Okla. Const. art. IX, § 18.
         9
           17 O.S. §§ 151–152.
         10
            Pub. Serv. Co. of Okla. v. Okla. Corp. Comm’n, 1996 OK 43, 918 P.2d 733, 738.


                                                                6
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 32




                 A tariff accommodating customer self-supply is an exercise of that authority when it

         governs the retail service furnished by the incumbent utility to customers within its certified

         territory. It may establish the rates, charges, contract terms, financial assurances, and conditions

         under which the incumbent provides retail service while recognizing that a customer has separately

         arranged for some or all of its generation requirements.

                 Such an arrangement need not certify a new retail supplier. It need not deregulate any retail

         service. It need not remove a customer from Commission-approved tariff service. Nor must it

         authorize a third party to furnish retail electric service within the incumbent's territory.

                 The relevant inquiry is whether the incumbent utility remains the retail electric supplier

         and whether the proposed tariff lawfully establishes the charges and conditions applicable to the

         services furnished. OG&E's contrary argument reduces to the proposition that a tariff which

         reduces or eliminates a generation-related charge for volumes a customer procures independently

         cannot constitute ratemaking, but instead amounts to electric restructuring. That proposition is

         incorrect.

                 Rate design routinely calibrates what a customer pays based on what services the customer

         takes. Time-of-use rates, interruptible credits, net metering, real-time pricing, and economic

         development riders all recognize that the rates applicable to a customer depend on the particular

         services provided and the costs incurred to provide them. Setting the utility generation charge at

         zero to reflect a customer's election to supply its own accredited generation capacity and reserve

         margin, while the tariff assigns the customer the delivery system costs attributable to the retail

         services it actually uses, is not electric restructuring. It is a cost-based price for the defined retail

         services taken under the incumbent's tariff.




                                                            7
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 32




                   The Commission's authority to evaluate such a tariff does not disappear merely because

         the customer procures generation through a wholesale market transaction. Whether a proposed rate

         schedule is just, reasonable, and consistent with cost causation is a question of rate design on the

         evidentiary record, not a categorical absence of jurisdiction or legal authority.

                   B. Self-supply or BYONG does not alter the incumbent utility's role as the retail
                   electric supplier

                   RESCTA regulates the furnishing of retail electric service (17 O.S. §§ 158.22(4),

         158.24(A)). Where a customer self-supplies SPP-accredited generation capacity for its load and

         the incumbent utility therefore furnishes no utility generation supply for that load, setting the retail

         generation charge to zero reflects the absence of utility generation service rather than a cessation

         of retail electric service. The incumbent utility continues to furnish retail delivery, transmission,

         metering, and billing services under its Commission-approved tariff, for which the customer

         remains obligated to pay.

                   Nothing in RESCTA conditions a utility's certificated retail supplier status on the

         incumbent utility generating or procuring one hundred percent of a customer’s energy

         requirements from the utility's own fleet. Where a customer satisfies its generation requirements

         through federally regulated wholesale market arrangements in SPP, the source of generation does

         not alter the identity of the incumbent utility furnishing retail delivery service.

                   C. Prior Commission orders limiting restructuring advocacy are not jurisdictional
                   holdings.

                   Opponents of self-supply have cited an order granting intervention in Case No. PUD2022-

         000093, which limited an intervenor’s participation to exclude advocacy in support of restructuring

         or deregulation.11 A ruling limiting the subjects an intervenor may advocate in a particular docket



         11
              Order No. 732023, Case No. PUD2022-000093 (Okla. Corp. Comm’n Feb. 7, 2023).


                                                               8
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 32




         is not a holding that the Commission lacks authority to approve a retail tariff for the incumbent’s

         own customers. That order confirms only that the Commission will not host a campaign for

         legislative restructuring inside a rate case. A self-supply or BYONG option asks for nothing of the

         kind.

              V. THE RETAIL ELECTRIC SUPPLIER CERTIFIED TERRITORY ACT DOES NOT
               CATEGORICALLY PROHIBIT CUSTOMER SELF-SUPPLY ARRANGEMENTS
                                          (ITEM (b))

                    A. RESCTA governs the identity of the retail electric supplier, not the source of
                    generation.

                    OG&E's characterization of customer self-supply as deregulation conflates two different

         concepts. Legislative restructuring would involve fundamental changes to the legal framework

         governing who may furnish retail electric service, including the potential introduction of

         competing retail suppliers into certificated territories or the removal of retail service from the

         Commission's existing regulatory jurisdiction. By contrast, a Commission-approved tariff that

         preserves the incumbent utility’s role as the lone certificated retail supplier, serving customers

         within its existing territory under its approved tariff, does not constitute deregulation.

                    RESCTA allocates service territories among retail electric suppliers and restricts a supplier

         from furnishing retail electric service to an electric-consuming facility located within another

         supplier's certified territory.12 The operative question under RESCTA is therefore straightforward:

         Who is furnishing retail electric service to the facility?

                    Under RESCTA (17 O.S. §§ 158.22(3)-(4), 158.24(A)), where OG&E continues to serve

         the customer within its certificated territory under a Commission-approved retail tariff, the

         customer's procurement of accredited wholesale generation capacity and energy in SPP does not

         violate RESCTA.


         12
              17 O.S. §§ 158.21–158.32.


                                                             9
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 32




                    Where the incumbent utility continues to deliver electricity over its facilities, meter the

         load, administer billing and the retail service agreement, and serve as the SPP Load Responsible

         Entity, it remains the exclusive retail electric supplier. A wholesale generation counterparty selling

         into SPP does not furnish retail electric service to the consuming facility.

                    B. RESCTA expressly excludes wholesale transactions from the definition of retail
                    electric service.

                    RESCTA defines retail electric service as “electric service furnished to a consumer for

         ultimate consumption but does not include wholesale electric energy furnished by an electric

         supplier to another electric supplier for resale.”13 The Legislature thus expressly distinguishes

         wholesale supplier transactions from retail electric service. A retail electric supplier, in turn, is an

         entity engaged in furnishing retail electric service.14

                    Because 17 O.S. § 158.22(4) expressly excludes wholesale electric energy transactions

         from the statutory definition of retail electric service, a wholesale generation counterparty selling

         into the SPP Integrated Marketplace or furnishing wholesale energy for resale is not a competing

         retail electric supplier as a matter of law.

                    C. Where no separate generation sale occurs at retail, RESCTA provides no basis to
                    infer an unauthorized competing retail supplier.

                    Whether a self-supply arrangement is structured through direct SPP Market Participant and

         Attachment AM Meter Agent attribution of accredited capacity to the incumbent utility as Load

         Responsible Entity, or through a bilateral wholesale pass-through sleeve administered by the

         incumbent utility, RESCTA is fully satisfied. Under either pathway, no third party sells or delivers

         retail electric energy to the consuming facility, the wholesale transaction is excluded from retail




         13
              17 O.S. § 158.22(4).
         14
              17 O.S. § 158.22(1).


                                                            10
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 32




         electric service under 17 O.S. § 158.22(4), and the incumbent utility remains the exclusive retail

         electric supplier charging cost-based retail delivery rates under its Commission-approved tariff.

                  D. The 2025 Oklahoma Supreme Court territorial decisions involved competing
                 retail suppliers, not customer-supported wholesale generation procurement.

                 In Oklahoma Gas & Electric Co. v. Oklahoma Corporation Commission, 2025 OK 43, and

         Oklahoma Electric Cooperative, Inc. v. Oklahoma Corporation Commission, 2025 OK 60, the

         Oklahoma Supreme Court addressed disputes involving competing retail electric suppliers and the

         protection of certificated service territories.15 Those disputes concerned which supplier could

         lawfully furnish retail service to particular consuming facilities.16 The disputes implicated the

         ability of one supplier to use transmission arrangements or other facilities to reach customers

         within another supplier's certified territory.

                 A materially different question arises when the incumbent utility continues to furnish retail

         service to its own customer in its own certificated territory under a Commission-approved tariff.

         Neither decision establishes that a certificated utility must itself generate or procure every kilowatt-

         hour associated with its customers' consumption. The Commission may preserve the exclusivity

         of certificated service territories while evaluating alternative generation procurement

         arrangements, such as self-supply or BYONG, that maintain the incumbent's retail service

         relationship. Those decisions address when one supplier may serve load in another supplier’s

         territory. They do not address a customer’s procurement of the commodity it consumes, and no

         Oklahoma decision does.




         15
            Oklahoma Gas & Electric Co. v. Oklahoma Corporation Commission, 2025 OK 43; Oklahoma Electric
         Cooperative, Inc. v. Oklahoma Corporation Commission, 2025 OK 60.
         16
            Id.


                                                            11
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 32




                 The Commission can give full effect to the Supreme Court's protection of certified

         territories while recognizing that an incumbent utility's retail service may be supported by different

         lawful generation procurement arrangements.

                VI. THIRD-PARTY SALES INTO ORGANIZED WHOLESALE MARKETS ARE
              SUBJECT TO FEDERAL JURISDICTION AND DO NOT BECOME RETAIL SALES
                     MERELY BECAUSE THEY SUPPORT CUSTOMER LOAD (ITEM (e))

                 A. The Federal Power Act establishes a jurisdictional distinction between wholesale
                 transactions and retail electric service.

                 The Federal Power Act grants FERC jurisdiction over the transmission of electric energy

         in interstate commerce and the sale of electric energy at wholesale in interstate commerce.17 The

         United States Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized the division of regulatory responsibility

         between federal and state authorities. In New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1, 19–20 (2002), the Court

         addressed the federal regulatory framework governing interstate transmission and wholesale

         transactions.18 In FERC v. Electric Power Supply Association, 577 U.S. 260, 266–68 (2016), the

         Court reaffirmed FERC's authority over practices directly affecting wholesale rates within the

         scope of the Federal Power Act.19 The filed-rate doctrine and principles of federal preemption

         likewise prohibit states from regulating or second-guessing FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rates.20

                 These authorities establish an important distinction for the Commission's consideration.

         The Commission retains authority over the retail service furnished by Oklahoma public utilities.

         FERC regulates wholesale sales and the operation of federally jurisdictional wholesale markets.

                  Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) is a FERC-approved Regional Transmission Organization

         responsible for coordinating the operation of the regional transmission system and administering

         17
            16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1).
         18
            New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1, 19–20 (2002).
         19
            FERC v. Electric Power Supply Association, 577 U.S. 260, 266–68 (2016).
         20
            See Nantahala Power & Light Co. v. Thornburg, 476 U.S. 953, 966 (1986); Mississippi Power & Light Co. v.
         Mississippi ex rel. Moore, 487 U.S. 354, 371–72 (1988); Hughes v. Talen Energy Marketing, LLC, 578 U.S. 150,
         154 (2016).


                                                               12
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 13 OF 32




         organized wholesale electricity markets. SPP provides transmission service under its FERC-

         jurisdictional Open Access Transmission Tariff and operates its Integrated Marketplace for the

         scheduling, dispatch, and settlement of wholesale electricity transactions.21 SPP, not OG&E,

         determines which generation plants are dispatched and when. FERC exercises regulatory oversight

         over SPP's jurisdictional tariff, including the rates, terms, and conditions governing interstate

         transmission service and wholesale-market rules.

                 SPP's role is significant because wholesale generation transactions do not require a separate

         transmission system connecting each generating resource to the retail customer whose load the

         resource supports. Generation may be scheduled and settled through SPP's wholesale markets

         using the regional transmission system. The incumbent utility may continue to furnish retail

         electric service under a Commission-approved tariff while the associated wholesale transactions

         remain subject to applicable FERC and SPP requirements.

                 The Commission's jurisdiction over the incumbent utility's retail rates and conditions of

         service is therefore distinct from FERC's jurisdiction over interstate transmission and wholesale-

         market transactions. The Commission may determine how the costs and benefits of a lawful

         wholesale generation arrangement are reflected in retail service without prescribing the wholesale

         rates or altering SPP's transmission and market rules. Accordingly, self-supply or BYONG

         arrangements may be accommodated through Commission-approved retail tariffs while the

         incumbent utility continues to furnish retail electric service.

                 B. Pre-Federal Power Act authority must be considered within the modern federal
                 jurisdictional framework.




         21
           Southwest Power Pool, Open Access Transmission Tariff, FERC Electric Tariff, Sixth Revised Volume No. 1; 18
         C.F.R. § 35.34.



                                                              13
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 32




                    In Southern Oklahoma Power Co. v. Corporation Commission, 1923 OK 939, 96 Okla. 53,

         220 P. 370, the Oklahoma Supreme Court addressed the application of Oklahoma's public utility

         laws to a private electric supply arrangement.22 However, that decision preceded the development

         of the modern federal regulatory framework governing interstate wholesale electricity transactions.

                    Southern Oklahoma Power was decided before the United States Supreme Court's decision

         in Public Utilities Commission of Rhode Island v. Attleboro Steam & Electric Co., 273 U.S. 83

         (1927), and Congress's enactment of the Federal Power Act in 1935.23 Those subsequent

         developments established the jurisdictional framework under which interstate wholesale electricity

         sales are subject to federal regulation, while retail electric service remains principally within state

         jurisdiction.

                    Accordingly, Southern Oklahoma Power must be considered in light of subsequent federal

         law. A decision predating the Federal Power Act cannot, standing alone, establish state regulatory

         jurisdiction over transactions now subject to FERC's exclusive wholesale jurisdiction. It also does

         not establish that a wholesale-market participant becomes a retail public utility merely because its

         generation supports an Oklahoma customer's load.

                    The Commission retains authority to regulate the retail rates, terms, and conditions of

         service furnished by incumbent utilities. That authority must be exercised consistently with

         FERC's jurisdiction over wholesale transactions. The two regulatory frameworks can operate

         together without treating self-supply or BYONG as categorically prohibited.

                    C. Wholesale counterparties are not Oklahoma “public utilities.”

                    Opponents have argued that any counterparty engaging with a self-supplying customer is

         furnishing power for ultimate consumption, is therefore a public utility under 17 O.S. § 151, and


         22
              Southern Oklahoma Power Co. v. Corporation Commission, 1923 OK 939, 96 Okla. 53, 220 P. 370.
         23
              Rhode Island v. Attleboro Steam & Electric Co., 273 U.S. 83 (1927).


                                                                14
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 15 OF 32




         would be subject to full Commission rate regulation. That theory is foreclosed by federal law. A

         counterparty selling capacity and energy in or through SPP’s markets sells at wholesale under

         FERC-jurisdictional tariffs or market-based rate authority. This Commission could not prescribe

         rates for those sales if it tried, and designating such a seller an Oklahoma public utility subject to

         rate regulation would conflict with the Federal Power Act.24 As discussed above, Southern

         Oklahoma Power cannot support state rate regulation of wholesale market participants today.

                    D. The on-premises exemption in 17 O.S. § 151 does not convert FERC-jurisdictional
                    wholesale generators in SPP into Oklahoma retail public utilities.

                    Self supply opponents (looking at you Shoop) also misread the parenthetical exemption in

         17 O.S. § 151 for power distributed by a producer solely on or through its own property for its

         own or its tenants' use. Section 151 defines when an entity furnishing retail power for public use

         in intrastate commerce is an Oklahoma public utility. A wholesale generator selling into the FERC-

         regulated SPP Integrated Marketplace is regulated exclusively by FERC under the Federal Power

         Act (16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1)) and is not furnishing retail electric service for public use under state

         law. The on-premises exemption in Section 151 simply exempts a retail landlord or industrial

         facility generating power on-site from state public utility regulation; it does not purport to, and

         under the Supremacy Clause could not, convert wholesale generators interconnected to the SPP

         transmission grid into regulated Oklahoma retail utilities.

         VII. HOUSE BILL 2992 SUPPORTS THE COMMISSION'S CONTINUED AUTHORITY
         TO DEVELOP APPROPRIATE LARGE LOAD SERVICE FRAMEWORKS (ITEMS (g),
                                        (h), AND (n))

                    A. HB 2992 establishes customer protections and Commission oversight; it does not
                    prohibit self-supply.




         24
              16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1); Nantahala, 476 U.S. at 966; Miss. Power & Light, 487 U.S. at 371-72.


                                                                   15
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 113 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 16 OF 32




                    House Bill 2992, the Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026, establishes

         a statutory framework for electric service to qualifying large load customers.25The legislation

         requires separate tariffs and terms and conditions of service for qualifying customers, establishes

         minimum contractual commitments, and directs attention to the costs and risks associated with

         serving exceptionally large electric loads. The statute reflects the Legislature's recognition that

         large load customers may present materially different service requirements from those associated

         with traditional customer classes. Such customers may require substantial generation capacity,

         transmission investment, and other infrastructure. They may also create unique risks associated

         with changes in projected load, early departure, or failure to satisfy contractual commitments.

                    HB 2992 responds to those circumstances by establishing statutory protections and

         preserving regulatory oversight. The statute does not, however, expressly prohibit self-supply or

         BYONG arrangements. HB 2992 also does not expressly require every qualifying large load

         customer to purchase all generation supply from the incumbent utility's existing generation

         portfolio.

                    HB 2992 does not independently create the Commission's authority to approve self-supply.

         The Commission's general authority to establish retail rates and conditions of service predates HB

                OG&E's rebuttal testimony characterizes the proposals advanced by intervenors as

                Under 17 O.S. § 190.3(8), retail wheeling means the transmission or distribution facilities

         of an electric utility being used to transport electric energy from a competing retail electric supplier

         to a retail electric consumer, with the third party making a retail sale and the utility acting only as

         a transporter for a fee. The definition matters, because a jurisdictional holding should not rest on

         a formulation a party has written for the occasion. A self-supply or BYONG option involves no

         retail sale by a third party and no transportation service rendered by the incumbent on any third

         party’s behalf to a retail customer. A properly designed option requires that all self-supply be

         coordinated with the incumbent and that all retail electric service be supplied through the

         incumbent. The third-party seller delivers into the SPP market at its settlement location; the

         incumbent, as the load-responsible entity, serves its retail customer’s entire load from the market

         and its own resources and bills the customer under its own tariff.

                    The contention that the incumbent is merely wheeling because it is “not generating” the

         energy its customer consumes substitutes a different test for the statutory one. A retail electric

         supplier does not cease to be the retail electric supplier because a portion of the energy its customer

         consumes was procured under a contract the supplier did not sign. Every utility in SPP serves its

         load in part with energy purchased in the Integrated Marketplace from generators it does not own;

         none of them is thereby wheeling to its own customers.

                    The retail wheeling objection also confronts a difficulty its proponents do not address. To

         the extent opponents insist that the self-supplied energy involves a wholesale sale and associated

         transmission service, those matters lie within FERC’s exclusive jurisdiction, and a state may not

         recharacterize them as retail.26 The objection is therefore either wrong on the facts or preempted

         on the law.

                    Nor does a self-supply option introduce retail competition. Oklahoma has not opened retail

         electric supply to competition. The Electric Restructuring Act of 1997 established a framework for

         studying a transition to customer choice, but its implementation was not carried forward, and

         Oklahoma retail customers today take service from the certificated supplier for their territory.

         Google does not contend otherwise, and a self-supply option does not depend on any restructuring

         authority. Retail competition means that a customer may choose among competing retail suppliers,

         utilities. That subsection defines “retail electric service distributor” and permits municipal utilities,

         access basis. The subject of the provision is the jurisdictional status of non-jurisdictional entities.

         legislative intent, not a rule that manufactures prohibitions from silence. It operates on parallel

         items within a common statutory subject; it does not permit the Commission to infer, from a

         definition governing municipal opt-in to open access, a prohibition on customer self-supply that

                A. Customer self-supply eliminates the incumbent utility's obligation to build,
                procure, or hold generation capacity for self-supplied load, and a certificate under
                RESCTA confers no right to compel customers to purchase utility generation (Item
                (f)).


                 Under Oklahoma law (17 O.S. §§ 152, 158.25), a regulated utility's service obligations are

         defined and bounded by the terms of its Commission-approved tariffs and the specific retail

         services a customer elects to take. When a large load customer elects to self-supply its generation

         requirements by providing SPP-accredited capacity sufficient to cover 100 percent of its peak load

         plus the applicable SPP Planning Reserve Margin, that election eliminates any obligation on the

         part of the incumbent utility to build, procure, or hold generation capacity for the self-supplied

         load. Because the customer satisfies the SPP resource adequacy requirement directly through its

         own accredited capacity and reserve margin, the incumbent utility's obligation is limited strictly to

         providing the retail transmission, delivery, metering, and billing services the customer actually

         takes and pays for under the tariff.

                 Nor does a certificated utility hold any statutory entitlement to force a customer to purchase

         utility-owned generation capacity that the customer does not use. A certificate of authority under

         RESCTA (17 O.S. § 158.25) grants an exclusive right against competing retail electric suppliers

         within the utility's certified territory; it does not confer a monopoly right to construct utility rate-

         base generation for load that a customer self-supplies with accredited capacity in SPP.

                 where no electric service is provided, while post-energization cost recovery is
                 governed by the tariff's contractual minimum bill structure (Item (i)).

         and 902, utility rates must be grounded in cost causation and compensate a utility only for electric

         service rendered using facilities that are used and useful in serving the public. In circumstances

                 The Commission possesses constitutional and statutory authority to establish the rates and

         exclusivity of certificated retail service territories but does not categorically prohibit wholesale

         generation transactions associated with a retail customer's load. The Federal Power Act recognizes

         the jurisdictional distinction between wholesale transactions and retail service. HB 2992

         establishes protections governing service to qualifying large load customers without expressly

         prohibiting appropriately structured wholesale generation procurement arrangements, such as self-

         supply or BYONG.

                 Together, these authorities establish that the Commission may consider a retail tariff

         accommodating self-supply or BYONG where the incumbent utility remains the certificated retail

         electric supplier and the arrangement otherwise complies with applicable law.

                 This conclusion does not authorize a competing retail supplier to furnish service within

         another utility's certified territory, nor does it relieve a large load customer of responsibility for the

         delivery system costs it causes. It simply recognizes that the Commission's existing ratemaking

         authority encompasses retail service arrangements that distinguish between generation supply

         procured by a customer in SPP and the retail delivery services furnished by the incumbent utility.

                 The Commission should therefore reject any categorical interpretation of Oklahoma law

         under which a self-supply or BYONG arrangement constitutes unauthorized retail wheeling,

         unlawful restructuring, or a violation of RESCTA.
